meta.tagline: The tropical stage of art deco pastels, cafecito steam and turquoise water

pills: An open-air museum of art deco

overview.title: Welcome to Miami
overview.intro: Miami is America's tropical exception: pastel art deco facades face a turquoise sea, Cuban coffee steam mingles with the clack of dominoes, and Wynwood's walls are repainted every year. Spanish is the unofficial first language here, salsa spills out of the supermarket, and the pastelito bakery open at 5 a.m. feeds the crowd leaving the nightclub. The beach is the shop window, but the city's heart beats in its Cuban, Haitian, Colombian and Venezuelan neighborhoods. Sunscreen and dancing shoes — Miami wants both in the same day. Dale!

local_word.definition: The multi-purpose command of Miami Spanish: 'let's go', 'okay', 'go ahead', 'keep going' — all at once. Pitbull's choruses carried it to the world, but it has lived on these streets for a century. The waiter taking your order, the friend pulling you to dance, the light turning green: dale. Crack this word and you've cracked Miami's rhythm.

rules.title: See South Beach, but find Miami in the neighborhoods
rules.description: Ocean Drive is for photos; the city's soul lives in Little Havana's domino park, on Wynwood's walls and under Coral Gables' banyan shade. Half a day for the beach, everything else for the neighborhoods — that's how Miami is loved.

rules.title: Join the cafecito hour
rules.description: Standing at a ventanita in mid-afternoon with a thimble of sweet espresso is Miami's shared ritual: watch the offices order a colada at 3:05 with the obligatory joke. The colada is for sharing — drinking one alone marks you as a tourist.

rules.title: Take the summer noon and the hurricane calendar seriously
rules.description: June to October is humid, showery and hurricane season: the afternoon rain comes and goes within the hour, and flexibility is enough insurance. Late October to May is the postcard Miami promises — in this city, date choice is half the experience.

quick_facts.label: Currency
quick_facts.sub: Check if service is already added

quick_facts.label: Language
quick_facts.sub: Spanish is the daily language here

tip.label: The Miami philosophy
tip.text: Here hurry loses to the midday sun and plans lose to the night's rhythm: beach in the morning, cafecito shade at noon, a long dinner, salsa at night. Schedule by rhythm, not by clock — dale, the rest arrives on its own.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Miami is a sprawling ribbon: a car or ride app is the base, the free Metromover is downtown's surprise, and the beach district walks on its own.

items.title: Arriving from the airport
items.description: MIA is 20–30 minutes from town and beach: ride apps are practical and taxis run flat rates to the beach. If you land at Fort Lauderdale, the Brightline train is the sleek, fast connection.

items.title: Metromover and Metrorail
items.description: Downtown's free elevated Metromover glides from Brickell to Bayside: a surprise gift for visitors. Metrorail serves the airport and Coconut Grove lines — no rail reaches the beach.

items.title: The car and the causeways
items.description: A car is essential between neighborhoods: the MacArthur Causeway crossing to the beach, lined with yachts and cruise ships, is the city's most beautiful drive. Parking in South Beach is pricey and gamed — use the garage apps.

items.title: Citi Bike and the beachwalk
items.description: The beachside path stretches north from Lummus Park: pedal in the morning cool with art deco facades for company. Within South Beach, a bike beats a car.

items.title: The boat perspective
items.description: Miami is another city from the water: Biscayne Bay cruises, boat rentals and the skyline seen from the waves. The sunset sailing serves the city's neon profile in golden light.

callout.label: Metromover tip
callout.text: When Downtown, board the Metromover and ride a loop: free, air-conditioned, and the view gliding between skyscrapers is surprisingly good. Get off at Brickell for a riverside lunch — Miami's most economical city tour.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Miami the choice is a choice of stage: South Beach's art deco window, Wynwood's wall art, Brickell's towers or the Grove's banyan shade.

local_word.definition: Miami's area code and identity card: '305 till I die' is the city's anthem of belonging. Locals introduce themselves with these three digits and songs are written on them. There's a newer 786 code too, but the heart's code never changes — 305 is the abbreviation of the Miami soul.

items.name: South Beach
items.description: Pastel hotels, Ocean Drive neon and the beach at the door: you wake up inside the Miami postcard. Brace for night noise — the calm-seeker should drift north to Mid-Beach.

items.name: Wynwood and Midtown
items.description: Mural walls, galleries, breweries and third-wave coffee: Miami's creative stage. Fifteen minutes to the beach by car — the young, characterful base.

items.name: Brickell
items.description: The financial district's skyscraper hotels, rooftop pools and riverside restaurants: modern Miami's center. Linked to Downtown by Metromover — practical for a city-first stay.

items.name: Around Little Havana
items.description: Calle Ocho's domino park, cigar workshops and coffee windows: daily life in Miami's truest neighborhood. Boutique lodging is limited, but the soul is matchless.

items.name: Coconut Grove
items.description: Sail masts on the bay, banyan-shaded streets and calm cafes: Miami's oldest, greenest neighborhood. The graceful choice for families and peace-seekers.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Miami's calendar is a bargain with humidity and hurricanes: December–April is the postcard, summer is the locals' test of patience, and late October is the turning point.

items.label: Spring
items.name: The Peak's Extension
items.subtitle: Spring · Warm sea, full beaches, festival rhythm
items.description: March and April are Miami at its fullest: spring breakers, music festivals and a perfect sea. May calms down as humidity starts to climb — for the balanced experience, late April to early May is the sweet spot.

callout.label: Spring break note
callout.text: In mid-March South Beach surrenders to the spring break crowd: prices soar and the nights peak in volume. In those weeks shift your stay to Mid-Beach, the Grove or Brickell — visit the beach, return to calm.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Humidity and Shower Season
items.subtitle: Summer · Humid heat, afternoon storms, hotel discounts
items.description: Summer Miami is humid and thundery: the afternoon downpour arrives like a ritual and passes, leaving steamy sun. Hotels hit their yearly lows — with a beach-morning, museum-noon, dinner-evening rhythm, summer works too.

callout.label: Hurricane note
callout.text: June to November is hurricane season, peaking August–October: travel insurance and flexible tickets are wise in these months. Keep a storm tracker on the phone — no warning means no panic; showers pass within the hour.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: The Turning Point
items.subtitle: Autumn · Breaking humidity, calm beaches, art season
items.description: In late October the humidity breaks and the city exhales: beaches calm, prices still friendly, galleries warming up before early December's Art Basel. November is the Miami of those in the know.

callout.label: Art Basel tip
callout.text: In early December Art Basel turns the city into the world's art stage: hotels sell out months ahead and prices multiply. Coming for the art, plan early; if not, skip that week — November offers the same city at half price.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Postcard Season
items.subtitle: Winter · 25°C sunshine, dry air, full terraces
items.description: Winter is Miami's promise: low humidity, clear skies, a swimmable sea. The frozen North pours in — prices peak, but they pay off: these are the weeks Miami was built for.

callout.label: January tip
callout.text: On a January morning hit the beach early: soft sun, clear water, the crowds still asleep. In the afternoon, cafecito and the domino park in Little Havana — winter Miami's ideal day is built from this pair.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: The Miami table is Latin America's meeting point: the crunch of the Cuban sandwich, the lime of the ceviche and the coffee cup passed through the ventanita.

local_word.definition: Cuban espresso whipped with sugar into a foamy crown: Miami's fuel. Drunk at the service window called a ventanita; the large shareable 'colada' comes with little plastic cups for distribution. 3:05 p.m. is the unofficial cafecito hour — join it and sync with the city.

items.name: The Cubano sandwich
items.description: Ham, roast pork, Swiss cheese, pickles and mustard, pressed hot in Cuban bread: the crunch is the mark of mastery. Try it at Little Havana's storied counters — the 'medianoche' version is the midnight classic.
items.tag: Press classic · listen for the crunch

items.name: The cafecito and pastelito ritual
items.description: Cafecito at the ventanita with a guava pastelito alongside: the official pair of the Miami morning (and afternoon). If you bought a colada, hand out the cups — sharing is the protocol itself.

items.name: The ropa vieja table
items.description: The shredded beef stew named 'old clothes': with black beans, rice and sweet fried plantains. The masterpiece of Cuban home cooking — Little Havana's portions are generous.

items.name: Stone crab season
items.description: From October to May, Florida's stone crab claws are served cold with mustard sauce: Miami's seasonal luxury. Claw size sets the price — if you're in season, don't miss it.

items.name: Ceviche and Latin fusion
items.description: Peruvian migration brought world-class ceviche to Miami: fresh fish, lime, ají pepper. The city's stylish rooms are the laboratory of Latin fusion — tiradito and arepa share a menu.

items.name: Cuban sweets and batidos
items.description: Tres leches, caramel flan and tropical batidos (shakes): where else will you taste guanabana or mamey? The sweet answer to a hot afternoon.

callout.label: Table rule
callout.text: When the bill arrives in Miami, check the 'gratuity included' line: many tourist venues add service automatically — don't tip twice on top. Never sit on Ocean Drive without asking menu prices and cocktail sizes; two streets in is both honest and delicious.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees Ocean Drive; these six are Miami's banyan-shaded, lighthouse-lit hidden face.

items.name: Vizcaya Museum and Gardens
items.description: An Italianate villa of 1916: marble terraces, labyrinth gardens and a stone barge descending to the bay. Miami's most graceful morning — go early for the light; stumbling into quinceañera photo shoots is part of the show.

items.name: The Venetian Pool
items.description: A 1924 public pool carved from a coral rock quarry in Coral Gables: waterfalls, grottoes and palms. The world's most beautiful municipal pool — go early on a summer morning.

items.name: Bill Baggs and the Key Biscayne lighthouse
items.description: Island calm twenty minutes over the causeway: an 1825 lighthouse, a waveless beach and picnic groves. The most peaceful address for gazing back at the Miami skyline.

items.name: Domino Park (Calle Ocho)
items.description: Máximo Gómez Park in the heart of Little Havana: masters in guayabera shirts slam dominoes all day as cigar smoke drifts. Watching is welcome, respect is essential — Miami's truest corner.

items.name: The MiMo Boulevard
items.description: Biscayne Boulevard's 1950s 'Miami Modern' motels with neon signs: restored lobbies, retro pools and photogenic facades. Art deco's lesser-known sibling — cruise the strip, stop at the signs.

items.name: Everglades Shark Valley
items.description: An hour west, the Everglades' 24-kilometer loop road: you cycle past alligators, and from the observation tower the 'river of grass' runs to the horizon. Miami's wild backyard — early morning, water bottle in hand.

callout.label: Shade strategy
callout.text: Miami's hidden corners negotiate with the sun: Vizcaya and the Venetian Pool in the morning, Domino Park in afternoon shade, MiMo at sunset neon. The Everglades is always morning work — the midday sun over the river of grass does not joke.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Miami's showcase is bright and its games are classic; know these four and invest your money in tables, not tricks.

items.name: The Ocean Drive cocktail game
items.description: Menus without prices, giant cocktails extended as 'happy hour', and a $45 surprise on the bill: Ocean Drive's oldest number.
items.instead: Ask menu prices and cocktail sizes before sitting; refuse the 'two-for-one' pitches. Take the view walking Ocean Drive, set your table on Española Way or two streets in.

items.name: The parking and tow trap
items.description: A wrong park in South Beach means a tow truck within minutes; some private lots run outrageous event-day pricing.
items.instead: Use the municipal garages and parking apps; read the sign to its last line. On beach days go early or arrive by ride app — a tow fee swallows the day's budget.

items.name: The cheap Everglades airboat tour
items.description: Some cut-price airboat tours end in a fifteen-minute noisy loop and shabby animal shows.
items.instead: Choose the national park side: the Shark Valley bike loop and ranger walks are authentic and economical. If you want an airboat, research a park-authorized, small-group operator.

items.name: The double-tip surprise
items.description: Tourist-zone restaurants add 18–20% service automatically; the unaware visitor writes another tip on top.
items.instead: Look for the 'gratuity/service included' line: if it's there, nothing more is needed — a few dollars if you're delighted. Make this check a Miami reflex, especially around Ocean Drive and Bayside.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In Miami the showcase's shine correlates with price, not with flavor or soul: the beach is free for everyone, the cafecito costs a dollar and change, the domino park costs nothing. Save the money for neighborhood tables and one boat ride — the 305 gifts you the rest.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Itineraries
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. Times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From pastel morning to salsa night

steps.title: South Beach morning
steps.description: Swim while the beach is empty and the light soft; then shoot Ocean Drive's art deco facades without the crowds.

steps.title: The art deco walk
steps.description: A pastel architecture tour via Española Way and Lincoln Road: facades, neon signs and shaded arcades.

steps.title: Little Havana lunch
steps.description: A Cubano on Calle Ocho, cafecito at a ventanita, the masters at Domino Park: Miami's heart lives in this triangle.

steps.title: The Wynwood walls
steps.description: A gallery-and-mural tour of the district: a different artist at every corner. The side streets outgive the main courtyard.

steps.title: Sunset on the bay
steps.description: Board a Bayside boat tour or sit on the Brickell riverside: the skyline turns neon in golden light.

steps.title: Salsa night
steps.description: Live Latin music in Little Havana or Brickell: mojito, ropa vieja and the dance floor. Dale — the night doesn't end early in Miami.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Beach, neighborhoods and the river of grass — the full Miami

steps.title: Classic Miami
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: beach morning, art deco, Little Havana, Wynwood, bay sunset, salsa.

steps.title: Gardens and island day
steps.description: Vizcaya's terraces in the morning; a marina-side lunch in Coconut Grove; Key Biscayne in the afternoon — the lighthouse and a calm beach; an evening around the Venetian Pool and a graceful Cuban dinner in Coral Gables.

steps.title: The Everglades and farewell
steps.description: An early Shark Valley bike loop — alligators and the tower; the MiMo Boulevard's retro motel signs on the way back; a farewell dinner of stone crab (in season) or ceviche — the last cafecito from a ventanita.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Miami lives bilingually; these five phrases are the key to joining the Spanglish rhythm.

items.meaning: Go / okay / let's do it — Miami's all-purpose command; you'll hear it fifty times a day
What's up? — the Cuban greeting; it opens doors in Little Havana
One cafecito, please — your most important sentence at the ventanita
Hey / listen — the warm Latin way of catching attention
The punctuation mark of Miami English — attachable to any sentence, bro
